habits.habits: All white, grayscale pages with one accent; a thin-ruled data table or ledger under the headline as the hero visual; a solid black main button paired with an underlined text link; a small gray reassurance line under the buttons (free, no card, cancel anytime); the same nav pattern (wordmark left, 4 links, dark pill button right); a big hero number in the table; one red or orange highlight for an over-budget or blocked row.

The least alike: sage, deep blue and near-black backgrounds, with different typefaces (heavy Korean gothic, serif, heavy grotesk). Shared habits remain: the headline sits beside or above a white or dark product card showing realistic sample data; a two-button pair (solid main button, outlined second button); a small reassurance line under the buttons; a 'trusted by' or footnote line at the bottom; one alert color for fee, blocked or over-budget items.

Every hero puts a full product dashboard in a bordered frame below the headline; a solid main button next to an outlined or text button; a small gray reassurance line under the buttons; a single accent color (green or teal) on a white page; the same nav pattern; a timeline or progress bar plus a big balance number in each mockup; the headline alignment changes (left, left, centered) but the stacking is the same.

The backgrounds differ (cream, dark green band, white) but the structure repeats: headline, then one line of supporting text, then a solid button and a text link, then a reassurance line, then a white card showing the product (timeline, budget summary, asset breakdown); the left column has a big number and the right a list; the same nav; one accent color; the Moa page is centered and plain, with a gray right panel.

Clearly one template: every hero is split, with headline and buttons on the left and a paper receipt card with a torn zigzag bottom edge on the right; the same red circular rubber stamp ('0원', 'DECIDED AUG 14', '$14 OVER'); monospaced numbers on the receipt; a muted tinted gray, blue-gray or sage page background; a black main button with an outlined second button; a reassurance line or key-value spec rows; a 'trusted by' logo strip below.

Tandem and Moa reuse the same split hero with a torn-edge receipt card and red circular stamp, monospaced figures, a pale gray background and a black-plus-outlined button pair; Pennywise breaks away with a centered headline and colorful rounded bento tiles (orange, lilac, mint, black), but keeps the same pill button pair and reassurance line; the same nav pattern and 'trusted by' strip.

Tandem and 모아 use the same device: a torn-edge paper receipt card set at a tilt, with a red circular rubber stamp, on a pale gray background beside a left-aligned headline. Every site has a solid black primary button next to an outlined 'See how it works' button, a small grey microcopy line under the CTAs, and the same nav layout. Pennywise's colorful bento cards set it apart a little, but its CTA pattern is still the same.

All three heroes are the same design. Each puts a white receipt card with a zigzag torn bottom edge and a red circular stamp beside the headline on a muted pastel background, in a two-column split; only the side the card sits on changes. All three use the same grotesk headline, a black primary button with an outlined secondary, monospace numbers in a ledger list, and a grey trust or microcopy line. Only the background tint and the language change.

Each layout has a hero, then a large product-UI card below it holding ledger rows of label and right-aligned figure. The nav is identical on all three, and each has a dark or green primary button with an underlined text link as the secondary. All three share the same small grey trust line, the same sample data (Lisbon, Austin, Lagos, Singapore; $1,148 of $3,200; 48,320,500원), and a red accent used for warnings. The color fields (deep green, white, beige) and the use of a timeline do differ.

All three use a hero with a full-width app mockup below it: a sidebar spec page, a tabbed asset dashboard, and a budget table. All three share the same green or black pill CTA paired with an outlined or text secondary, a grey microcopy line about the trial or no fees, the same nav, and a red or orange 'over' or 'blocked' flag. The typefaces really do differ: a wide grotesk, a Korean serif and a centered serif, which hides some of the template.

The color and type choices are genuinely different: sage with a heavy Korean display face, a dark theme with a mint button, and royal blue with a serif and a yellow button. The underlying pattern still repeats, though: a product card (receipt-style list, budget table or spec card with a timestamp list) next to or under the headline, a primary and secondary CTA pair, a microcopy line of trial and encryption notes, and the same sample data and nav.

All three are white pages with thin black hairline rules and tables in bordered boxes: a ledger of asset categories, a budget table, and a timeline grid of updates. Each uses a solid black or teal block button with an underlined text link as the secondary, a grey microcopy line of dot-separated facts, the same nav, and red text for overspend or blocked items. The headline faces vary (sans, serif, extended grotesk) and the alignment varies, but the overall look is the same restrained table-based one.

lost.text: Neither is weaker on direction: the two share an identical first screen and the same editorial serif plus ledger-table look built around Pennywise's left-to-spend budget, and the full pages differ only in pricing-table wording, where Y spells out "Not included" instead of a bare dash and names the plan in its button ("Try Plus free for 30 days"), which is why Y ships.

Neither version is weaker on direction: they share the same editorial serif, ledger-style budget table and plain black-and-white palette, and differ only in small pricing-table details. Y's bare dashes for features Basic lacks are less clear than X's explicit 'Not included'.

The two screenshots match except for the async-standups section, where X uses a generic stack of quoted lines and even puts quotation marks around names like "Priya Shah · Lisbon", while Y turns the updates into city-tagged cards with teal rules and an orange rule for the blocked one, carrying over the hero's time-zone timeline look.

In Y, the async-standups section loses X's row of teammate standup cards with their city labels and blocked-status accents, and turns them into a list of quoted names that copies the pain-point section above, so the page's main time-zone product artifact becomes generic text.

Both share the same passbook-ledger serif direction, but X breaks the '입출금·예적금' label onto two lines in the hero table and uses a generic '무료로 시작하기' CTA, while Y keeps the label on one line and uses a CTA specific to the product, '앱 받고 1분 만에 연결하기'.

Y uses a generic "무료로 시작하기" CTA instead of X's product-specific "앱 받고 1분 만에 연결하기", and its hero ledger wraps "입출금·예적금" onto two lines, which breaks the clean passbook-row rhythm the concept depends on.
X uses the same serif-and-ledger look, but its overspend nudge is just a red status line instead of a row you can act on ("Move $14"), so it shows less of what the product actually does.
Y squeezes the product's nudge into a cramped red status cell and drops the header CTA and trust line, so the ledger reads more like a generic table than a budgeting coach that suggests a next move.

X is missing a brand mark, and its timeline bars don't line up with their local times (Jonah's 07:40 update starts at 06). That weakens the page's one idea, mapping updates across time zones, which Y gets right and backs with the logo and the highlighted 'is blocked'.

Y drops the interlocking-rings logo mark and the orange 'is blocked' highlight, and its update bars no longer start at each teammate's posted local time, so the time-zone timeline feels more generic and less tied to Tandem's 'no 6am call' story.

Neither is weaker on direction: both use the same passbook-ledger concept, serif headline and monochrome table, so the gap is only in polish, where Y adds a header download button, a more specific call to action and a trust line, though its ledger runs past the first screen.

Y drops the MyData/no-fee trust line and the transfer and alert rows inside the ledger, so its bankbook gets more generic, though it frames the whole ledger neatly within the first screen, which X's cut-off table doesn't.

X shows a plain category table with no per-category progress bars, so the hero mockup reads like a generic spreadsheet rather than this app's own envelope-style budget view, and its "before November starts" headline contradicts the in-progress November budget shown right below it.

Y removes the per-category spend bars that made the hero's budget table read as a budgeting tool, so its type and palette could belong to any dark fintech; it also says 'before November starts' when the page shows it is already November, and a white band cuts off the bottom of the first screen.

X has the same navy, yellow and serif look, but it has no logo mark and its decision card has no 'agreed async by Design, Eng & PM' line or orange 'blocked' highlight, so less of it is tied to Tandem's async-decision story.

Y drops the interlocking-rings Tandem mark, the 'agreed async by Design, Eng & PM' decision line, the orange 'blocked' accent and the 'nobody has to be online at the same time' promise, and those were the details that tied the look to this async-collaboration brand, so it reads as a generic navy SaaS hero (it also loses the Sign in link and the customer trust strip).

Both versions share the same art direction: the heavy Korean display headline, the sage background, the red 0원 accent and the fee-comparison transfer card, so neither has weaker direction; Y is the better ship because it adds navigation and a reassurance line under the CTA, while X has no nav.

Neither is weaker: both use the same Moa layout, with the heavy display headline, the sage and vermilion palette, and the fee-comparison receipt card. Y drops the nav and the sign-up reassurance line, which costs usability but leaves the art direction unchanged.

Neither version is weaker: X and Y are byte-identical files (same checksums for both the fold and full-page shots), so they share the same Tandem-specific direction, built around the time-zone standup log, the decision record and the 'give your team its mornings back' framing.

Neither is weaker on direction, since the two pages are pixel-identical apart from the Plus pricing button, which says 'Try Plus free for 30 days' in X and 'Start 30-day free trial' in Y; X's label names the plan you're picking, so it reads a little clearer.

Neither is weaker: both carry the same Tandem-specific direction, with a timezone timeline of teammates' local-time updates, warm off-white and forest-green palette, and async-first copy, and the folds and full pages look identical.

I can't tell the two apart: the first-screen images are byte-identical, and the full pages look the same at review size, so neither has weaker direction (both keep the Tandem time-zone timeline, decision log and the 'mornings back' story).

Neither version has weaker direction: both share the same restrained monochrome look with a serif headline and a ledger-style asset card, and Y only drops X's reassurance line under the buttons (no sign-up or monthly fee, one-minute account linking, MyData-based) and the header divider, which costs some trust and structure but does not change the art direction.

The art direction is the same in both: the same restrained black-and-white editorial serif look, the same ledger-style budget mock-up and the same copy, so neither is weaker; X just has rougher details, with a centered table that breaks the ledger's left-aligned reading line and a broken, wrapped 'Start free' button on the Basic pricing card.

Neither version is weaker: X and Y are byte-identical files (matching checksums for both fold and full), so they share the same Tandem-specific look of time-zone timelines, an async decision log and the 'nobody online at the same time' headline.

Neither version is weaker on direction: they share the same serif headline, deep-green fintech palette, product mockup and section layout, and differ only in the main button's label, where Y's '무료로 앱 받기' says exactly what happens next and matches the '앱 다운로드' nav button, while X's '무료로 시작하기' is vaguer.

Neither version has weaker direction: they share the same serif-led Korean headline, deep green palette and product-dashboard hero, and differ only in the primary CTA label, where Y's generic '무료로 시작하기' is less precise than X's '무료로 앱 받기', which matches the app-download action.

Neither is weaker: both use the same editorial serif and monochrome ledger look, so the only differences are polish, and Y wins there because its table and summary are left-aligned and easier to scan, despite redundant subhead copy that leaves 'hours.' alone on the last line.

Neither is weaker: both use the same editorial serif and monochrome ledger look tied to Pennywise's 'budget honest' idea, but Y centers the category names and the on-track note inside the table, which makes it slower to scan than X's left-aligned rows, even though Y's shorter subhead avoids X's one-word last line.

Neither version has weaker direction: both use the same wide grotesk headline, the same green and the same product mock that tracks a spec across time zones; Y only adds green to part of the headline and cuts subcopy that repeats it, which tidies the page without changing its look.

Neither version has weaker direction: both share the same serif headline, deep-green palette and asset-dashboard mockup, and differ only in the CTA row, where Y's single primary button and trust line make for a clearer hierarchy.

Neither version has weaker direction: both share the same serif Korean headline, deep-green palette and live asset-dashboard mockup, and differ only in the CTA row (X has one primary button, a text link and a trust line; Y has App Store and Google Play buttons and shows more of the mockup).
